plain_english: Whatever you put serious effort into, you naturally come to love. So do people put serious effort into bad things? No. Do they put effort into things that don't matter to them at all? No, not those either. That leaves only one option: people put serious effort into things they think are good. And if you work hard at something, you love it. So whoever truly understands what's good can also know how to love properly. But someone who can't tell good from bad, or neutral things from either — how could they know how to love? Real love only belongs to the wise.
original_excerpt: What a man applies himself to earnestly, that he naturally loves. Do men then apply themselves earnestly to the things which are bad? By no means. Well, do they apply themselves to things which in no way concern themselves? Not to these either. It remains then that they employ themselves earnestly only about things which are good; and if they are earnestly employed about things, they love such things also. Whoever then understands what is good can also know how to love; but he who cannot distinguish good from bad, and things which are neither good nor bad from both, how can he possess the power of loving? To love, then, is only in the power of the wise.

plain_english: Don't fool yourself about this universal truth: every living creature cares about nothing more than its own interests. Whatever seems to block those interests — whether it's a brother, father, child, beloved, or lover — it will hate, reject, and curse. By nature, we love nothing more than our own interests. Our interests become our father, brother, family, country, and God. So when the gods seem to stand in our way, we curse them. We tear down their statues and burn their temples. Just like Alexander ordered the temples of Aesculapius burned when his dear friend died.
original_excerpt: For universally, be not deceived, every animal is attached to nothing so much as to its own interests. Whatever then appears to it an impediment to this interest, whether this be a brother, or a father, or a child, or beloved, or lover, it hates, spurns, curses; for its nature is to love nothing so much as its own interests: this is father, and brother, and kinsman, and country, and God. When then the gods appear to us to be an impediment to this, we abuse them and throw down their statues and burn their temples, as Alexander ordered the temples of Aesculapius to be burned when his dear friend died.

plain_english: Here's the point: if you put your self-interest in the same place as your values — your sense of what's sacred, good, and right, along with your duties to country, parents, and friends — then all of these are protected. But if you put your self-interest in one place and your friends, country, family, and justice in another place, all the good things get crushed under the weight of self-interest. Whatever you consider most important — that's where your attention goes. If you think your body matters most, that's where your focus goes. If you think your choices matter most, that's where it goes. If you think external things matter most, that's where it goes. Only when I place myself where my will is — only then will I be the kind of friend I should be, the kind of son and father I should be. Because then it will be in my interest to stay faithful, modest, patient, self-controlled, and helpful. It will be in my interest to do right by everyone in my life. But if I put myself in one place and honesty in another, then Epicurus wins. His teaching says either there is no such thing as real virtue, or virtue is just whatever people happen to think is virtuous.
original_excerpt: For this reason, if a man put in the same place his interest, sanctity, goodness, and country, and parents, and friends, all these are secured: but if he puts in one place his interest, in another his friends, and his country and his kinsmen and justice itself, all these give way, being borne down by the weight of interest. For where the I and the Mine are placed, to that place of necessity the animal inclines; if in the flesh, there is the ruling power; if in the will, it is there; and if it is in externals, it is there. If then I am there where my will is, then only shall I be a friend such as I ought to be, and son, and father; for this will be my interest, to maintain the character of fidelity, of modesty, of patience, of abstinence, of active co-operation, of observing my relations (towards all). But if I put myself in one place, and honesty in another, then the doctrine of Epicurus becomes strong, which asserts either that there is no honesty or it is that which opinion holds to be honest (virtuous).

plain_english: All these wars happened because of ignorance. The Athenians fought the Spartans. The Thebans fought both of them. The Persian king fought the Greeks. The Macedonians fought everyone. The Romans fought the Getae. And long before that, the Trojan War happened for the same reasons. Alexander was Menelaus's guest. If you had seen how friendly they were, you would never have believed anyone who said they weren't friends. But then someone threw a piece of meat between them — like you'd do with dogs. That meat was a beautiful woman. And over her, war broke out. Now when you see brothers acting friendly and seeming to agree on everything, don't assume anything about their friendship. Don't trust them even if they swear oaths and say nothing could ever separate them. You can't trust the mind of a bad person. It's unstable. It has no reliable principles to guide it. Different things overpower it at different times.
original_excerpt: It was through this ignorance that the Athenians and the Lacedaemonians quarrelled, and the Thebans with both; and the great king quarrelled with Hellas, and the Macedonians with both: and the Romans with the Getae. And still earlier the Trojan war happened for these reasons. Alexander was the guest of Menelaus, and if any man had seen their friendly disposition, he would not have believed any one who said that they were not friends. But there was cast between them (as between dogs) a bit of meat, a handsome woman, and about her war arose. And now when you see brothers to be friends appearing to have one mind, do not conclude from this anything about their friendship, not even if they swear it and say that it is impossible for them to be separated from one another. For the ruling principle of a bad man cannot be trusted; it is insecure, has no certain rule by which it is directed, and is overpowered at different times by different appearances.

plain_english: Don't judge people by whether they share the same parents or grew up together or had the same teacher. Judge them by this alone: where do they put their focus? Do they care about external things or about their own will and choices? If they focus on externals, don't call them friends. Don't call them trustworthy, steady, brave, or free. Don't even call them human beings if you have any sense. It's not human nature that makes people attack each other, abuse each other, and fight over empty land or public spaces like wild animals. It's not human nature that makes them rob each other in courtrooms. It's not human nature that makes them lustful, unfaithful, and corrupt. It's not human nature that drives all the terrible things people do to each other. There's only one thing behind all this bad behavior: they put themselves and their interests in things they can't actually control.
original_excerpt: But examine, not what other men examine, if they are born of the same parents and brought up together, and under the same pedagogue; but examine this only, wherein they place their interest, whether in externals or in the will. If in externals, do not name them friends, no more than name them trustworthy or constant, or brave or free; do not name them even men, if you have any judgment. For that is not a principle of human nature which makes them bite one another, and abuse one another, and occupy deserted places or public places, as if they were mountains, and in the courts of justice display the acts of robbers; nor yet that which makes them intemperate and adulterers and corrupters, nor that which makes them do whatever else men do against one another through this one opinion only, that of placing themselves and their interests in the things which are not within the power of their will.

plain_english: But if you discover that these people truly believe good exists only where there is proper intention and right judgment, then don't worry about whether they're your father, son, brothers, or long-time companions. Once you've confirmed this one thing about them, you can confidently call them friends. You can say they're trustworthy and just. Where else does friendship exist except where you find loyalty, decency, and shared commitment to honest things — and nothing else?
original_excerpt: But if you hear that in truth these men think the good to be only there, where will is, and where there is a right use of appearances, no longer trouble yourself whether they are father or son, or brothers, or have associated a long time and are companions, but when you have ascertained this only, confidently declare that they are friends, as you declare that they are faithful, that they are just. For where else is friendship than where there is fidelity, and modesty, where there is a communion of honest things and of nothing else.

plain_english: But you might say, "He treated me well for so long — didn't he love me?" How do you know, you fool, that he didn't regard you the same way he uses a sponge to clean his shoes? Or the way he takes care of his livestock? How do you know that once you stop being useful to him, he won't toss you aside like a broken dish? "But this woman is my wife, and we've been together so long." And how long did Eriphyle live with Amphiaraus? She was his wife and the mother of his children. But a necklace came between them. And what is a necklace? It's just our opinion about such things. That was the animal instinct at work. That's what destroyed the friendship between husband and wife. That's what stopped the woman from being a wife and the mother from being a mother.
original_excerpt: But you may say, Such a one treated me with regard so long; and did he not love me? How do you know, slave, if he did not regard you in the same way as he wipes his shoes with a sponge, or as he takes care of his beast? How do you know, when you have ceased to be useful as a vessel, he will not throw you away like a broken platter? But this woman is my wife, and we have lived together so long. And how long did Eriphyle live with Amphiaraus, and was the mother of children and of many? But a necklace came between them: and what is a necklace? It is the opinion about such things. That was the bestial principle, that was the thing which broke asunder the friendship between husband and wife, that which did not allow the woman to be a wife nor the mother to be a mother.

plain_english: If you want to be a true friend or have true friends, you need to tear out certain poisonous opinions. Hate them. Drive them out of your soul. When you do this, first you'll stop beating yourself up. You won't fight with yourself anymore. You won't keep changing your mind. You won't torture yourself. Second, you'll be a complete and genuine friend to others who think like you. You'll also be patient with people who think differently. You'll be kind to them, gentle, ready to forgive them because they're ignorant and confused about what really matters. You won't be harsh with anyone, because you know Plato was right: no one chooses to be wrong. If you can't manage this, sure, you can still hang out like friends do. You can drink together, live together, travel together. You might even be born from the same parents, just like snakes are. But you won't actually be friends — neither will they — as long as you hold onto these savage and damaging beliefs.
original_excerpt: And let every man among you who has seriously resolved either to be a friend himself or to have another for his friend, cut out these opinions, hate them, drive them from his soul. And thus first of all he will not reproach himself, he will not be at variance with himself, he will not change his mind, he will not torture himself. In the next place, to another also, who is like himself, he will be altogether and completely a friend. But he will bear with the man who is unlike himself, he will be kind to him, gentle, ready to pardon on account of his ignorance, on account of his being mistaken in things of the greatest importance; but he will be harsh to no man, being well convinced of Plato's doctrine that every mind is deprived of truth unwillingly. If you cannot do this, yet you can do in all other respects as friends do, drink together, and lodge together, and sail together, and you may be born of the same parents, for snakes also are: but neither will they be friends, nor you, so long as you retain these bestial and cursed opinions.
